title: The Evidence That Birds Are Dinosaurs
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The claim that birds are dinosaurs is not a comparison or a figure of speech. It is a statement about descent: that birds sit inside the theropod group, in the way that bats sit inside the mammals, and it is now the mainstream position.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first line of evidence is skeletal and it is old. Thomas Huxley noticed in the 1860s that the hind limb of a chicken and the hind limb of certain dinosaurs share features that no other group has, and the list has since grown considerably.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Particular structures do the heaviest work. The furcula, the fused collarbone a diner calls a wishbone, is present in theropods long before any bird; so is a hollow-boned skeleton; so is a wrist bone shaped to let the hand fold sideways, which is the motion a wing makes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second line arrived in the 1990s, from a deposit in northeastern China where fine volcanic ash preserved soft tissue. The fossils there carry filaments, and in some specimens unambiguous branched feathers, on animals that could not fly and were not birds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That matters because of what it removes. Before those finds, feathers could be treated as the thing that made a bird a bird, and afterwards feathers are a theropod feature that birds inherited along with everything else.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A third line concerns behaviour, which is harder to fossilise and more persuasive when it does. Specimens of Citipati have been found sitting on nests, limbs folded over the eggs in the posture a brooding bird uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fourth is physiological, inferred from bone. Birds have an unusual breathing system with air sacs extending into hollow spaces in the skeleton, and those same spaces, in the same bones, appear in theropods that lived tens of millions of years earlier.

paras.label: H
paras.text: No one of these would carry the claim. Skeletal similarity alone could be convergence, feathers alone could be a coincidence of preservation, and a single nesting fossil could be an animal that died on a meal. Four independent lines agreeing is a different kind of argument.

theropod: the group of dinosaurs within which birds sit, in the way bats sit within mammals.

Describe the connection between the wrist bone and the motion of a wing.

note: RI.9-10.1 at this grade means evidence from four disciplines that do not share a method. Ask which line a student would give up first and what the claim would survive on.

title: Who Built Stonehenge
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Stonehenge was raised in stages over roughly fifteen hundred years, by people who left no writing. Everything claimed about them is inferred from material, and the inferences have become far stronger in the last thirty years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The stones themselves carry an origin. The smaller bluestones were matched by their chemistry to specific outcrops in the Preseli Hills in west Wales, around two hundred and forty kilometres away, and some quarry faces there show working.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The large sarsens were sourced more recently. A core removed during a repair in 1958 and returned decades later allowed a chemical comparison that placed most of them at West Woods in Wiltshire, about twenty-five kilometres from the site.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is a claim about stone. The claim about people requires different material, and the richest source is a settlement at Durrington Walls, a short distance away, occupied while the monument was being built.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What survives there is rubbish, which for an archaeologist is better than treasure. Vast quantities of animal bone, broken pottery and hearths record what was eaten, in what season and in what quantity, by people who were not farming at the time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Isotopes in the teeth of those animals carry the decisive detail. The chemistry of an animal's teeth records the geology of the place it grew up, and the pigs and cattle eaten at Durrington came from across Britain, some from hundreds of kilometres away.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Human remains point the same way. A burial near the site, known as the Amesbury Archer, has tooth chemistry consistent with a childhood in the Alpine region, which says nothing about who built the monument and a great deal about how far people moved.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Assembled, the lines support a specific inference and refuse a looser one. They support people travelling long distances and gathering seasonally to build; they do not identify a single group, a purpose or a belief, and a confident account of why it was built is reaching past what the material holds.

isotope: a form of an element whose proportions vary by region, so that teeth record where an animal grew up.
outcrop: a place where a particular rock reaches the surface, allowing stone to be matched to a source.
Describe the connection between what the evidence supports and what it refuses.
questions.a: The lines support people travelling long distances and gathering seasonally to build, and they do not identify a single group, a purpose or a belief, so a confident account of why it was built reaches past the material.

note: Paragraph H is the discipline the standard is really asking for. Students will want the purpose, and the article declines to supply what the evidence cannot.

title: Measuring the Distance to a Star
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Nothing about a star tells you directly how far away it is. A bright star may be luminous and distant or faint and close, and the two cases look identical from the ground.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The only direct method is geometric. As the earth moves around the sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the background of far more distant ones, and the size of that shift gives the distance by trigonometry.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shift is minute. Friedrich Bessel measured the first one in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni, and the angle involved is roughly what a coin would subtend from several kilometres away, which is why the measurement waited for the nineteenth century.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Parallax also runs out. Beyond a certain distance the shift is smaller than the instrument can resolve, so the method that is trustworthy because it rests on geometry alone covers only the nearest part of the problem.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The next rung depends on a particular kind of star. Henrietta Swan Leavitt established that certain variable stars pulse at a rate related to their true brightness, so measuring the period of one gives its luminosity, and comparing that with how bright it looks gives distance.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The relation had to be calibrated, and this is where the ladder becomes a ladder. The period and brightness relation gives relative distances on its own, and converting those into kilometres requires knowing the true distance of at least one such star, which comes from parallax.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A third rung extends further again. A particular kind of exploding star reaches a known peak brightness, and that brightness is calibrated against galaxies whose distances are already known from variable stars, which were themselves calibrated by parallax.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The structure is the point. Each rung is checked against the rung below, an error at the bottom propagates all the way up, and the figure for the most distant object depends on a trigonometric measurement of a star a few light years away.

Summarize how astronomical distances are established.
questions.a: Parallax measures a nearby star's apparent shift as the earth orbits and gives distance by trigonometry, but it runs out beyond a certain range. Variable stars whose pulse rate relates to true brightness extend the reach, though converting their relative distances into kilometres requires a parallax measurement, and exploding stars of known peak brightness extend it again, each rung calibrated by the one below.

parallax: the apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background as the observer moves.
luminosity: how much light a star actually emits, as distinct from how bright it appears from here.
Describe the connection between the lowest rung and the most distant measurement.
questions.a: Each rung is calibrated against the one below, so the figure for the most distant object depends on a trigonometric measurement of a star a few light years away.

note: Thorough evidence here means a chain where every link carries the ones above it. Ask what happens to the furthest figure if the parallax of one nearby star is revised.

title: The Court Records of a Village
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most people who have ever lived left no written trace of themselves. They did not write, nobody wrote about them, and the documents that survive from their societies are about taxation, landholding and the affairs of people who mattered.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There are exceptions, and they are nearly always accidental. A record created for an entirely different purpose occasionally captures ordinary lives in detail, because the purpose required asking questions nobody otherwise asked.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Court records are the richest of these. A proceeding has to establish what happened, which means recording who was where, who saw it, what time it was, what the weather was doing and who was owed money by whom.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An inquisition register from a village in the Pyrenees in the 1320s is the best-known example. It was made to identify heresy, which required interrogating almost everyone about their households, their movements, their neighbours and their beliefs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result is a document of extraordinary depth and obvious distortion. Hundreds of people describe their own lives in their own words, and every word was spoken under compulsion to an official who could imprison them.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Using it well means separating what the register was trying to establish from what it incidentally recorded. A statement about belief was the point of the question and is the least reliable part; a statement about who was in the house that evening was incidental and is far more trustworthy.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That distinction generalises to almost every official source. The thing a document was built to capture has been shaped by whoever built it, and the details it captured by accident were not worth distorting to anybody.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the strongest evidence a record contains is frequently not its subject. A tax roll is weak evidence about wealth and strong evidence about who lived next to whom, and a historian reading for the second is using the document against its own grain deliberately.

Summarize why records made for other purposes are valuable evidence.
questions.a: Most people left no written trace, and the records that capture them were made for other reasons, such as an inquisition register that interrogated a village about households and movements in order to identify heresy. What the document set out to establish is the least reliable part because it was shaped by its makers, while the incidental detail was not worth distorting to anyone.

questions.q:
incidental: recorded in passing rather than as the purpose of a document, which is what makes it trustworthy.
against the grain: reading a source for something other than what it was made to record.
Describe the connection between a detail being incidental and its being reliable.
questions.a: The thing a document was built to capture has been shaped by whoever built it, and the details it captured by accident were not worth distorting to anybody.

note: The generalisation in paragraph G is the transferable part. Apply it to a school's own records and ask what they are accidentally strong evidence about.

title: How a Drug Is Shown to Work
standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Showing that a treatment works is harder than it sounds, and the difficulty is not technical. Most people given most treatments improve, improvement is the thing everybody involved was hoping for, and the question is therefore never whether patients got better but whether the treatment is why.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Conditions fluctuate, people seek help when they feel worst, and expecting to improve produces measurable change. A study that compares patients before and after cannot distinguish a drug from any of those.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So the first requirement is a comparison group receiving something else, and the second is that the two groups be alike at the start. Allocating by chance achieves that, because randomness distributes both known and unknown differences evenly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third requirement is less obvious and is where many studies fail. The person enrolling patients must not know which group the next patient will go to, because a clinician who can predict the allocation can steer sicker patients toward the comparison.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is blinding. If patients know what they received, their reports of how they feel are affected, and if assessors know, their judgements of ambiguous findings shift in a direction nobody intends and nobody notices.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A fifth concerns what is counted. Patients who stop taking a drug are often those it suited least, so analysing only those who completed the course compares the people who tolerated the treatment with everybody in the other group.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The sixth is registration. A trial that states its main outcome in advance cannot later report whichever of twelve measures came out best, and comparing a published paper with its registration is a check anybody can run.

paras.label: H
paras.text: None of these is about the drug. They are about the ways a comparison can be spoiled, and a trial is really a set of defences against the specific errors that produce a positive result when there is nothing there.

questions.a: Patients who stop are often those the drug suited least, so analysing only those who completed compares the people who tolerated the treatment with everybody in the other group.

note: Each requirement answers a named failure. Have students match the six defences to the six ways a result could be wrong without anyone lying.

title: The Discovery That Ulcers Are Infectious
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of the twentieth century stomach ulcers were understood as a disease of stress and acid, and the understanding was not idle speculation but a framework with a treatment attached. The treatment was to reduce acid, it relieved symptoms reliably, and the ulcers very often came back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as evidence against the explanation. A patient whose ulcer returned had a chronic disease, and nothing in the framework suggested that the return was telling anyone something.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In 1979 a pathologist in Perth, Robin Warren, noticed curved bacteria in biopsies from inflamed stomachs. The observation was unremarkable except that the stomach was believed too acidic for bacteria to survive in.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Barry Marshall, then a trainee, began collecting cases with him. The bacteria appeared consistently in patients with inflammation and ulcers, and the association held across a series large enough that coincidence became an uncomfortable explanation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: An association was not going to be enough, and they knew precisely why. Bacteria might colonise damaged tissue rather than cause the damage, so finding them in an ulcer is consistent with their being a consequence of it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Attempts to produce the disease in animals failed. In 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the organism himself, developed gastritis within days, had it confirmed by biopsy, and then treated it with antibiotics.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A self-experiment with one subject, unblinded and unrandomised, is weak evidence by every standard that normally applies to anything. Its force came from what it predicted rather than from what it showed: if the bacterium causes the disease, then antibiotics should cure ulcers, and controlled trials showed that they did.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea therefore shifts twice. It begins as a story about a surprising observation, becomes a story about why an observation is not enough, and ends as a story about a prediction that could have failed and did not.

questions.a: Ulcers were explained by stress and acid, and recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as counter-evidence. biopsy: a sample of tissue taken for examination, which is where the bacteria were seen.

questions.a: The recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as evidence against the acid explanation, so nothing in the framework suggested the return was telling anyone something.

note: Paragraph B is the quiet one and the important one. An explanation that absorbs its own failures is the thing students should learn to notice.

title: The Enclosure of the Commons
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: For centuries much of England was farmed in open fields, under an arrangement that looks chaotic on a map and was not. A household held scattered strips across several large fields, and alongside them held rights over common land: to graze animals, gather fuel, cut turf or glean the grain left after a harvest.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Those rights were not ownership and they were not charity. They were customary entitlements attached to a holding, recognised in manorial courts, and for a household at the margin they were frequently the difference between sufficiency and destitution.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Enclosure replaced that arrangement with consolidated private holdings. It happened gradually by agreement over several centuries and then rapidly by statute, with several thousand individual Acts of Parliament passed between the mid-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agricultural case for it was real. Consolidated fields permit drainage, selective breeding and crop rotation that scattered strips cannot, and output per acre on enclosed land rose measurably.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distributional consequence was also real and fell on different people. A household whose entitlement was customary rather than documented had difficulty establishing it before commissioners, and compensation when granted was often a plot too small to be viable.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The central idea is therefore not that enclosure was efficient or that it was unjust. It is that the same change was both, and that the gains and the losses were not experienced by the same households.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A further detail refines it again. Many smallholders who received an allotment sold it within a generation, because an enclosed holding carried costs that a commons right did not, principally the obligation to fence it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why the episode is argued about still. It is a case where a measurable improvement in output and a measurable loss of security are both documented, and any summary that reports one of them has summarised half the evidence.

title: The Ozone Hole
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ozone high in the atmosphere absorbs a band of ultraviolet light that damages living tissue, and it is the only thing that does. The layer is thin, it is distributed unevenly across latitudes and seasons, and until the 1970s nobody had a reason to think anything human was affecting it at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1974 Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland published a chemical argument rather than an observation. Chlorofluorocarbons are so stable that nothing destroys them in the lower atmosphere, so they drift upward, and ultraviolet light eventually breaks them apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The products are destructive out of proportion to their quantity. A released chlorine atom can catalyse the destruction of ozone repeatedly without being consumed, so a small amount of gas removes a large amount of ozone over time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The prediction was for gradual thinning spread across the globe. That is what the chemistry implied, and it is what the argument was debated as, and the chemical industry's response addressed that version of the claim.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What was found in 1985 was something else. A British team working at Halley Bay in Antarctica reported a severe seasonal loss over the pole, far larger and far more localised than the theory had predicted.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The observation nearly did not surface. Satellite instruments had been recording the same low values and the processing software was discarding them as errors, on the reasonable ground that readings that extreme usually indicate a malfunction.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The explanation required a mechanism nobody had included. Ice clouds that form only in the extreme cold of the polar winter provide surfaces on which chlorine compounds convert into forms that destroy ozone rapidly when the sun returns.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea develops through three stages and is different at each. A prediction from pure chemistry, an observation that did not match it, and a mechanism that explained why the observation was worse than the prediction and confined to one place.

title: The Standard Gauge
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The distance between the rails on most of the world's railways is an awkward figure: four feet eight and a half inches. It is not a round number in any system, and nothing about it was calculated.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It descends from the wagonways that served collieries in the north of England, where horse-drawn wagons ran on rails to the river. George Stephenson built his early locomotives for lines of roughly that width, and his engines were the ones other companies bought.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Competitors chose differently and had reasons. Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western at just over seven feet, arguing correctly that a wider gauge permits greater stability, higher speed and a larger loading area.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The technical argument was not the one that settled it. Where two gauges met, every passenger had to change trains and every item of freight had to be unloaded and reloaded, and that cost fell on anyone shipping anything across the join.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is a different kind of problem from an engineering problem. The value of a gauge depends on how many other lines use it, so the better system loses to the more common one once the network is large enough.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Britain legislated in 1846, specifying the narrower gauge for new passenger lines, and the Great Western converted the last of its broad gauge in 1892. In the United States the conversion was largely completed over two days in 1886, with crews moving one rail inward along thousands of kilometres of track.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The central idea refines as it goes. It begins as a story about an arbitrary measurement, becomes a story about why the better design lost, and ends as a story about a property that belongs to networks rather than to things.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That property has not gone anywhere. Keyboards, electrical plugs, file formats and shipping containers are all cases where the arrangement in use is the one that was adopted early, and the question of whether it is the best arrangement is close to irrelevant.

title: The Green Revolution
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of the twentieth century a number of countries were expected to be unable to feed themselves within a generation. Population was rising faster than yields, the arithmetic was straightforward, and the projections were widely published, widely believed and taken seriously by the governments they concerned.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What changed the projection was plant breeding. Norman Borlaug and others developed wheat and then rice varieties that were short-stemmed, which sounds like a small detail and is the centre of the whole thing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A tall cereal given plenty of fertiliser grows a heavy head and falls over, which ruins the crop. A short-stemmed plant can carry a much heavier head without lodging, so it can convert fertiliser into grain rather than into stem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The yields that followed were not incremental. Wheat output in India and Pakistan roughly doubled within a decade, and the famines that had been forecast for the 1970s did not occur on anything like the predicted scale.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The central idea at that point is a technical success, and the article could stop there. The detail that complicates it is that the new varieties only outperform the old ones under particular conditions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: They require fertiliser, reliable water and often pesticide. A farmer with irrigation and access to credit gains enormously; a farmer on rain-fed land without credit gains little and may be worse off as prices fall with the larger harvest.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the same innovation widened a gap while closing another. Aggregate production rose decisively and the distribution of who benefited followed the distribution of irrigation and lending, which was not even.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The environmental account arrived later again, and it is still being written. Decades of intensive irrigation have drawn down groundwater in several of the regions where the gains were largest, which means that part of the increase was not produced at all but borrowed, from a stock that is not being replaced at anything like the rate it is used.

title: How an Outbreak Is Investigated
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An outbreak investigation has a prescribed sequence, set out in training materials and followed by public health agencies everywhere, and the sequence is not a formality. Each step produces the material the next one needs, and performing them in a different order produces answers that cannot be relied on afterwards.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first step is to establish that there is an outbreak at all. More cases than usual is a comparison, which requires knowing what usual was, and a rise can be produced by a new test, a new doctor or a new reason to look.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is to write a case definition, in advance and in writing. It states the symptoms, the place and the period that qualify someone as a case, and it is fixed before anyone starts counting.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That order matters more than it appears. A definition written after cases are known can be shaped, deliberately or not, around the people already suspected, and every count made with it will then confirm what produced it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third step is descriptive: count the cases by time, by place and by person. The resulting curve of cases against date distinguishes a single common source, which produces one sharp peak, from person-to-person spread, which produces successive waves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only now is a hypothesis formed, and the order is the whole discipline. The description constrains what can be proposed, so a hypothesis arrived at this way has already survived a test it did not choose.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The fourth step tests it comparatively. Cases are compared with non-cases from the same population, asking what each was exposed to, and an exposure common to cases and rare among the others becomes the candidate.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The fifth is confirmation by a different method entirely, such as finding the organism in the suspected food or water. An epidemiological association and a laboratory finding are independent, and the investigation is considered closed when they agree.

title: How a Budget Is Assembled
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A public budget arrives as a single document and is produced by a process that runs for most of a year. The order of that process determines what is possible to change and when, which is rarely obvious from the document.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins with a forecast rather than a plan. Officials estimate what revenue will be available under existing arrangements, and that figure constrains everything afterwards without having been chosen by anybody.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next comes the baseline, which is the cost of continuing to do exactly what is already being done. It is not a neutral quantity: it embeds every past decision, and it typically rises on its own through pay, prices and the number of people entitled to a service.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The gap between the forecast and the baseline is the real subject of the exercise. Departments are asked to bid against a total that is already allocated to continuing commitments, and the sum available for anything new is what remains.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bids are then prepared, and the sequence rewards particular behaviour. A department asked to propose reductions will propose ones that are visible and unpopular, because a reduction that nobody notices invites the question of why it was not made earlier.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Decisions are taken late and quickly. The final allocations are frequently settled in a short period near the end, which means that the options considered are the ones that survived the earlier stages rather than the best ones available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Publication comes last and is the first thing the public sees. A reader meeting the document at that point is looking at the output of six months of narrowing, with no record of what was excluded at each stage.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why a budget debate rarely changes a budget. By the time the figures are public the process that produced them has finished, and an argument about a line item is an argument about the last stage of a sequence that was mostly decided earlier.

paras.text: Publication comes last and is the first thing the public sees. A reader meeting the document then is looking at the output of six months of narrowing, with no record of what was excluded along the way.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why a budget debate rarely changes a budget. By the time the figures are public the process is finished. An argument about a line item is an argument about the last stage of a sequence mostly decided earlier.

questions.q: Why is the baseline not a neutral quantity?
questions.a: It embeds every past decision and typically rises on its own through pay, prices and the number of people entitled to a service.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why departments propose visible reductions) and paragraph H (i.e. why a budget debate rarely changes a budget).

questions.a: A revenue forecast made under existing arrangements constrains everything, then a baseline costing current commitments is set, and the gap between them is what departments bid against. The sequence rewards proposing visible reductions, final allocations are settled quickly near the end from options that survived earlier stages, and publication comes last, so public debate addresses a process already finished.

questions.q:
baseline: the cost of continuing existing commitments unchanged, against which new bids are measured.
allocation: the portion of a total assigned to a particular department or purpose.

questions.a: By the time the figures are public the process that produced them has finished, so an argument about a line item addresses the last stage of a sequence that was mostly decided earlier.

note: The order is the argument here, as in the outbreak article. Ask at which stage a student would have to intervene to change an outcome.

title: How a Theorem Is Proved
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mathematical paper is organised in a way that looks backwards to anyone expecting an account of how the work was actually done. It begins with definitions, proceeds through a series of small results that nobody outside the paper cares about, and reaches the theorem it is named for somewhere near the end.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That order is not chronological. Mathematicians typically start from the result they want and work toward what would establish it, and the paper presents the reverse of the route actually taken.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is that a proof is a check rather than a narrative. A reader has to be able to verify each step using only what precedes it, and an account in discovery order would require accepting things before they had been established.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So the definitions come first because nothing can be said without them. A definition in mathematics is not an explanation of a familiar word; it is a stipulation that creates the object, and everything later depends on its exact form.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then come lemmas: small results established on the way, each proved from the definitions and from earlier lemmas. Individually they are usually uninteresting, and collectively they are the structure the theorem stands on.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The main theorem is then often short. Having built the lemmas, the proof of the central claim can be a few lines, because the work was done in the pieces that came before it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The order also determines what a counterexample does. A proof is a chain, so an error anywhere breaks everything after it, and the standard question a reader asks is not whether the conclusion is plausible but which line first fails to follow.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading one therefore means reading for dependency rather than for narrative. The useful question at every line is what earlier statement makes this permissible, and a line that depends on nothing stated above it is where the paper is wrong.

title: How a Law Is Drafted
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A government decides to do something, and some months or years later a statute appears. Between those two events is a drafting process, largely invisible from outside, whose order shapes the law that results more than most of the public debate about it does.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins with instructions rather than text. A department sets out what it wants to achieve, in ordinary language, and sends that to specialist drafters, and the quality of the instructions determines most of what follows.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The drafter's first question is usually one nobody in the department asked. What exactly counts as the thing being regulated, who precisely does the obligation fall on, and what happens in the case the policy did not consider.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those questions produce the definitions section, and the definitions are written before the operative provisions because the provisions cannot be written without them. A rule about vehicles requires a boundary around the word.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then come the duties, in a deliberate order: who must do what, by when, subject to which exceptions, enforced by whom, with what consequence for failure. Each of those is a separate decision and each is capable of hollowing out the one before it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An exception drafted broadly can undo the duty it attaches to without appearing to. A provision requiring something except where it is not reasonably practicable may be a sensible limit or a complete escape, and which it is depends on words settled at this stage.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Consequential amendments come near the end. A new statute usually interacts with existing ones, and the schedule listing changes to other legislation is often longer than the Act itself and is read by almost nobody.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Debate arrives after all of it. Legislators argue about the policy, in language from the instructions, while the provisions that will decide cases were settled earlier by people whose names do not appear on anything.

title: How a Species Is Named
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Naming a newly recognised organism is governed by rules that are closer to law than to biology. They determine which of several proposed names is correct, and correctness here has almost nothing to do with whether a name is apt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first requirement is a type specimen. One particular individual, physically preserved and deposited in a collection anyone can consult, becomes the permanent anchor of the name, and the name refers to whatever group that specimen belongs to.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That order is the opposite of what people expect. A name is not attached to a description that organisms may or may not fit; it is attached to an object, and the description is a claim about what else resembles it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The consequence appears when a species is later split. If the group turns out to be two, the original name stays with whichever one contains the type specimen, and the other requires a new name regardless of which is more numerous or better known.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second requirement is publication in a form the rules recognise, with a date. Priority then governs: where two names have been published for the same organism, the earlier one is correct, and the later becomes a synonym.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Priority produces outcomes that nobody likes and the system accepts anyway. A familiar name can be displaced by an obscure earlier description found in a nineteenth-century journal, and the rules provide limited routes to prevent it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The point of all this is stability rather than accuracy. A name that means whatever its describer intended would change with every revision of opinion, and a name anchored to an object in a drawer does not.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the sequence encodes a decision about what names are for. Specimen, then publication, then priority, and the name is a label with a physical referent rather than a summary of what anybody currently believes.

title: The Language of a Safety Data Sheet
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Every hazardous chemical in a workplace arrives with a document in a fixed sixteen-section format. It is written to be found in an emergency, in a hurry, by somebody who has never read that particular sheet before and may never read another, and almost every feature of it follows from that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The order is prescribed and never varies. Identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, and so on down to regulatory information, so a reader looking for first aid knows it is section four before opening anything.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The vocabulary is more constrained than ordinary technical writing. Hazard statements are drawn from a fixed catalogue, each with a code, so causes severe skin burns and eye damage is one specific statement rather than a description somebody composed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That standardisation has a purpose beyond tidiness. Identical wording across manufacturers and languages means a translation is a lookup rather than an interpretation, and a worker who has learned what a statement means has learned it for every product.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Signal words are reduced to two. Danger marks the more severe category and Warning the less severe, and no third option exists, which prevents a manufacturer from softening a classification through phrasing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The sheet also distinguishes hazard from risk, and the distinction is frequently misread. A hazard is a property of the substance and does not depend on circumstances; the risk depends on how much, how often and under what controls.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a sheet can look alarming for something handled routinely. Vinegar has hazard statements, and the statements describe what concentrated acetic acid can do, not what is likely while dressing a salad.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a document that reads as flat and uninflected. That is deliberate: emphasis would be a judgement by the writer, and a format that allows emphasis allows a manufacturer to decide what a reader notices first.

title: The Language of a Peace Agreement
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A negotiated settlement has to be signed by parties who disagree about what happened and about what should happen next. The text has to be acceptable to all of them, and most of its characteristic features follow from that requirement.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The most important is constructive ambiguity, and it is deliberate rather than careless. A phrase that each side can read as supporting its own position allows an agreement to be signed where a precise phrase would prevent one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: This is a genuine technique with a genuine cost. The dispute has not been resolved, it has been postponed and relocated into the interpretation of a clause, and it will reappear when the clause has to be applied.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Verbs are chosen for how much they bind. Shall creates an obligation, will is weaker and often read as an expectation, and should is close to advisory, and the difference between them is frequently the subject of the longest arguments in a negotiation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Sequence words carry as much weight as verbs. Whether a clause reads after elections or following the establishment of conditions determines whether anything is actually required to happen by a particular time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The naming of parties is itself contested. A document that names an entity may be read as recognising it, so agreements are often drafted to describe parties by role, or by the places they control, rather than by the names they call themselves.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Even the title does work. Agreement, accord, framework, declaration and memorandum carry different implications about whether a binding instrument has been created, and the choice is usually made late and argued about hard.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a text that reads as evasive to an outsider and is precise about a different thing than the reader expects. It is not vague about the dispute; it is exact about what each party has agreed to be bound by, which is less.

title: What Engineers Mean by Failure
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary use, failure means something broke and somebody is at fault. In engineering it means a component stopped performing its intended function, and the two meanings pull hard against each other whenever an engineer speaks in public.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A designed structure has a failure mode, which is not a fault but a plan. The engineer decides in advance which part will give way first and how, because a structure that fails in an unpredicted manner fails in the most dangerous one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A related term is factor of safety. It is the ratio between the load a thing can take and the load it is expected to take, and a value of three does not mean two thirds of the structure is wasted.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It means the design absorbs variation nobody can measure in advance: the material that came in slightly below specification, the load nobody anticipated, the corrosion that accumulated, the installation done imperfectly on a wet afternoon.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Ductile and brittle are the next pair, and the distinction matters more than almost any other. A ductile failure deforms visibly before it gives way, and a brittle one separates without warning, and a design is frequently chosen to make failure ductile rather than to make it less likely.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Redundancy is similarly misread. In ordinary language it means something surplus to requirements; in engineering it means a second path for a load if the first one goes, and calling it surplus is exactly the reasoning that removes it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fail-safe is not a thing that cannot fail. It is a thing whose failure leaves the system in a safe state, such as a brake held off by pressure, which engages when the pressure is lost rather than releasing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is that an engineer discussing failure in public is routinely misheard. Saying a structure is designed to fail in a particular way sounds like an admission and is a description of the safest available arrangement.

paras.text: Ductile and brittle come next, and the distinction matters more than almost any other. A ductile failure deforms visibly before giving way. A brittle one separates without warning. Designs are often chosen to make failure ductile rather than less likely.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Redundancy is misread the same way. In ordinary language it means surplus to requirements. In engineering it means a second path for a load if the first one goes. Calling it surplus is exactly the reasoning that removes it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fail-safe is not a thing that cannot fail. It is a thing whose failure leaves the system safe, such as a brake held off by pressure, which engages when the pressure is lost rather than releasing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So an engineer discussing failure in public is routinely misheard. Saying a structure is designed to fail in a particular way sounds like an admission. It is a description of the safest available arrangement.

questions.q: What does a factor of safety absorb?
questions.a: Variation nobody can measure in advance: material below specification, an unanticipated load, accumulated corrosion and imperfect installation.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. ductile and brittle failure) and paragraph G (i.e. what a fail-safe actually is).
Summarize the technical meanings of failure and the terms around it.
questions.a: In engineering a failure is a component ceasing to perform its function, and a failure mode is a plan for which part gives way first, because unpredicted failure is the most dangerous kind. A factor of safety absorbs unmeasurable variation, a ductile failure deforms visibly while a brittle one gives no warning, redundancy is a second load path, and a fail-safe fails into a safe state.

questions.q:
ductile: deforming visibly before giving way, which gives warning that a brittle failure does not.
redundancy: a second path for a load, which ordinary language mistakes for something surplus.
Describe the connection between calling redundancy surplus and removing it.
questions.a: In ordinary language redundancy means something surplus to requirements, and calling it surplus is exactly the reasoning that removes a second load path.

note: Every term here has an everyday meaning that is close enough to be dangerous. Ask which misunderstanding would do the most damage in a public inquiry.

title: The Language of a Reference
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A written reference for a former employee is constrained in ways that make it almost unreadable by ordinary standards, and the constraints are not the writer's choice. They come from law, from institutional policy, and from the fact that the subject of the reference may eventually be entitled to see it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In many jurisdictions a reference must be fair and accurate, and a statement that damages someone can be actionable if it cannot be supported. That produces a strong incentive to say only what can be documented.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The result is a register built from verifiable facts. Dates of employment, job title, duties as recorded, and attendance figures, each of which can be defended from a file and none of which answers the question the reader is asking.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many large organisations have reduced the problem by removing the judgement entirely. They provide only confirmation of the facts, as policy, which protects the organisation and transfers the difficulty onto whoever must now decide without information.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Where evaluation survives, it is read as a code. Experienced readers treat the absence of a positive statement as the message, so a reference describing someone as punctual and nothing else is understood to be saying something it has not said.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That reading is unreliable in both directions. A writer who is simply terse, or following a template, produces a document indistinguishable from a deliberate signal, and the reader has no way to tell which they are holding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further asymmetry worth noticing. The subject of the reference usually cannot see it at the time it matters, so a misreading that harms them is a misreading they are not able to correct.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a genre that satisfies nobody. The writer cannot say what they think, the reader cannot learn what they need, and both continue to participate because the alternative is a document with no standing at all.

title: What a Statistician Means by Random
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary speech random means arbitrary, unexpected or without pattern. In statistics it means produced by a process whose outcomes have known probabilities, which is nearly the opposite of without pattern.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A random sample is not a haphazard one. It is a sample drawn by a procedure in which every member of a population had a specified chance of being selected, and that specification is what makes the sample useful.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Stopping people in a shopping street is haphazard and is not random in this sense. Nobody can say what chance a given person had of being approached, so nothing can be calculated about how the sample relates to the population.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This is why a very large haphazard sample is worth less than a small properly drawn one. Size reduces one kind of error and does nothing to the other, and a biased sample of a million is confidently wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Randomness is also a property of a process rather than of a result. A sequence of ten heads can be produced by a fair coin, and judging a process by whether its output looks patternless is a reliable way to be mistaken in both directions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: People are poor at producing it and poor at recognising it. Asked to write a random sequence, most produce one with too few repetitions, because a run of four looks wrong, and genuine randomness produces runs more often than intuition allows.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further technical use of the word in experiments. Random assignment means allocation by a chance process, and its purpose is specifically to distribute unknown differences evenly, which no deliberate procedure can do.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a word that means almost the reverse of its everyday sense. Ordinary random means nobody chose; statistical random means the choosing was done by a specified process whose properties are known, which is a strong condition rather than an absence of one.

title: The Introduction of a Paper
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The introduction to a research paper is three or four paragraphs long and has a shape so consistent that a reader can predict where each sentence is going before reading it. The shape is sometimes called a funnel, and the name is accurate.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens wide. The first sentences establish that an area of work exists and matters, in terms a reader from a neighbouring field could follow, and they are frequently the only sentences in the paper written for a general audience.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then narrows to what is known. A paragraph summarises the established findings, with citations, and the summary is selective, because the author is assembling the particular background against which their own claim will look necessary.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The narrowing continues to what is not known. A sentence appears beginning however, or despite this, or it remains unclear whether, and that sentence is the hinge on which the entire paper turns.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That gap is constructed rather than discovered. There are always many things not known about any subject, and the author has selected the one their study happens to address, which is legitimate and is worth seeing clearly.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The final sentences state what the paper does. Here we show, or this study examines, and in most journals the last sentence of the introduction is the paper's claim in its most compressed form.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The structure therefore does a particular job. By the time a reader reaches the methods they have accepted that a question matters, that it is open, and that the approach taken is the reasonable one, and none of those was argued for.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A useful exercise is to read the introduction backwards, one paragraph at a time. Start at the claim, then move up to the gap, and ask whether the gap identified is the one that actually blocks the field or simply the one this study was already in a position to fill.

title: The First Chapter of a History
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first chapter of a serious history book is rarely the start of the story. It is usually an argument about what the story is, and a reader who treats it as throat-clearing has skipped the part that determines everything after.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It generally does four things. It states the question, defines the period, explains why the existing accounts are inadequate, and announces what this book will do differently, in that order and with varying degrees of politeness.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The definition of the period is the least obvious and most consequential. A history of a revolution that begins ten years earlier than the usual date has made a claim about causes before describing a single event.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The engagement with existing work is where the argument becomes explicit. A historian names the accounts they are writing against, summarises them fairly enough to be credible, and identifies what each one could not explain.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That summary deserves checking. A book's account of its rivals is written by someone with a reason to find them insufficient, and a reader who learns a field from one book's first chapter has learned one historian's map of it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The announcement of method matters as much. A historian saying they will use estate records rather than parliamentary debates has told a reader which people will appear in the book and which will not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Everything after is then shaped by those commitments. The chapters follow the period as defined, the evidence is of the kind announced, and the conclusion answers the question stated on page four rather than any other question.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the first chapter is the place to argue with a book, and almost nobody does. By chapter six the framework is doing its work invisibly, and a reader who accepted the period, the sources and the question has already conceded most of what was ever in dispute.

title: The Discussion Section
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The discussion is the last substantial section of a research paper and the one where its claim can grow. The results section states what was measured; the discussion says what it means, and the distance between those is where the paper is most vulnerable.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens by restating the finding, usually in a single sentence and usually with the hedges intact. That sentence is worth comparing with the one in the abstract, because the two are often not the same claim.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then places the finding among existing work. Studies that agree are cited, studies that disagree are explained, and the explanation for disagreement is frequently a methodological difference the author is in no position to verify.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Next comes the mechanism, and this is where a correlational study often acquires a cause. A paragraph proposing how the effect might work is legitimate, and a reader who carries that proposal back to the result has upgraded an association without noticing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The limitations paragraph follows, and its placement does something. Coming after the mechanism, it is read against a claim the paragraph before has already strengthened, rather than against the narrower thing actually measured.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then come implications, which is where the widening is most visible. A finding in one population at one time becomes a statement about practice, and the verbs change from past to present as it happens.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The closing sentences usually call for further research. That is uninformative on its own, and it is worth asking what specific study the authors are describing, because a precise call and a vague one say different things about how firm the finding is.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The useful comparison is therefore between two sentences a few pages apart. Take the result as stated in the results section, take the claim in the final paragraph, and the gap between them is what the discussion added rather than found.

title: The Executive Summary
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A long report opens with a summary of two or three pages. It is written last, it is read first, and for most of its audience it is the only part that is read at all, which gives it a peculiar status within the document.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is not an abstract in the scientific sense. An abstract describes a paper; an executive summary is meant to be usable on its own, so it must restate the findings rather than refer to them and must stand without the body behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That independence creates the characteristic problem. A summary that works alone cannot carry the qualifications that make the findings defensible, and a summary that carries them is too long to be read by the people it was written for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What gets dropped is predictable. Sample sizes, the basis of estimates, the range around a central figure and the conditions a recommendation depends on are the first to go, because each costs a clause and none changes the headline.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The recommendations are the part most likely to travel further. They are extracted, pasted into other documents and acted on, and they arrive in those documents without the finding they rest on, let alone its conditions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A well-made summary resists this in a specific way. It attaches the condition to the recommendation in the same sentence, so that the two cannot be separated by a careless copy, which is the only form of protection available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is also a structural tell worth knowing. A summary whose recommendations are not traceable to specific findings in the body is a summary where someone has added a conclusion the evidence section does not contain.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the summary is where the report is most used and least examined. Comparing each of its claims against the section it came from takes an afternoon and is the most reliable way to find out whether a report says what it is being quoted as saying.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a structural tell worth knowing. A summary whose recommendations cannot be traced to specific findings in the body is one where somebody has added a conclusion the evidence section does not contain.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the summary is where a report is most used and least examined. Comparing each claim against the section it came from takes an afternoon. It is the most reliable way to learn whether a report says what it is quoted as saying.

questions.q: Why can an executive summary not carry its own qualifications?
questions.a: A summary that works alone cannot carry the qualifications that make the findings defensible, and one that carries them is too long to be read by the people it was written for.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. attaching conditions to recommendations) and paragraph G (i.e. the structural tell).

questions.a: It is written last, read first, and often alone, so it must restate findings without the body, which means sample sizes, estimate bases, ranges and conditions are dropped. Recommendations are extracted and acted on without the findings beneath them, so a good summary ties a condition to a recommendation in one sentence, and recommendations not traceable to findings signal an added conclusion.

questions.q:
qualification: a condition limiting a finding, which a short summary tends to drop.
traceable: able to be followed back to a specific finding in the body of a report.
Describe the connection between a recommendation travelling and the condition it depends on.
questions.a: Recommendations are extracted, pasted into other documents and acted on, arriving without the finding they rest on, let alone its conditions.

note: The check in paragraph H is the practical one. Take a real report, trace five summary claims to their sections, and count how many narrow on the way.

title: The Caveats at the End of a Model
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A model of a climate, an epidemic or an economy produces numbers, and the numbers are what gets reported. At the end of the document that produced them there is a section nobody quotes, and it is where the numbers are explained.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first thing it usually says is that these are projections and not predictions. A projection states what follows if stated assumptions hold, and a prediction states what will happen, and a model produces only the first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The assumptions are then listed, and the list is the model. A climate model runs several scenarios of future emissions, and the difference between its outputs is mostly the difference between those scenarios rather than anything about the physics.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This means a single reported figure has usually had a scenario chosen for it. Which one was selected is a decision by whoever wrote the summary, and the highest and lowest are frequently both defensible and far apart.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The caveats also describe what the model does not contain. A model of an epidemic may not represent behaviour change, so its figures describe what happens if nobody responds, which is a condition that has never once held.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That omission is not a flaw and is frequently the point. A projection assuming no response is built to show why a response is needed, and quoting it as a forecast of deaths misrepresents it precisely by taking it seriously.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Uncertainty is given in the same section and in a particular form. A range is not a confidence that the truth lies inside it; it is the spread produced by the runs that were performed, and a factor nobody modelled lies outside the range entirely.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the claim a model supports is refined almost entirely at the end. The figure in the headline is the output, the conditions attached to it are the claim, and the two are published in the same document and almost never in the same place.

title: The Expert Witness
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An expert witness occupies a position that is structurally strange. They are paid by one side in a dispute, they are called because their opinion assists that side, and their formal duty is owed to the court rather than to whoever is paying.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That duty is not decorative. In many jurisdictions it is stated in rules and in a declaration the expert signs, requiring them to give an independent opinion and to say plainly where a question falls outside their expertise.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The rhetoric of a good expert report follows from that duty. It states the material it was given, the material it was not given, the assumptions it proceeds on and the points on which a reasonable expert could take a different view.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those concessions are not weakness. An expert who concedes nothing is easier to attack, because an opponent need only find one overstatement to put the whole opinion in question, and a report that marks its own edges has removed that opportunity.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structural problem lies before any of this. Each side selects its expert, and a party that consults three and instructs the one most favourable has produced a sympathetic witness without anyone saying anything untrue.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The effect at trial is predictable. Two qualified experts testify to incompatible conclusions, and a jury with no means of evaluating the field is left deciding between them on manner, confidence and clarity.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some courts have changed the procedure in response. Experts may be required to meet before trial and produce a joint statement of what they agree on and precisely where they differ, which moves the disagreement into a narrower space.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What that reveals is how much of the dispute was real. Two experts who agree on nine points and differ on the tenth have given a court something usable, and the adversarial version of the same evidence would have presented it as total disagreement.

title: The Budget Speech
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A finance minister presenting a budget is performing a document that already exists. The figures were settled weeks earlier, the speech cannot change them, and everything in the delivery is about how they will be understood.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The order is the first instrument. Announcements that cost nothing and sound generous come early, and measures that take money arrive later, when a listener has already formed an impression of what kind of budget this is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Numbers are selected for their frame. A figure can be given as a total, as an annual amount, as a share of spending or as an increase over a previous year, and the same policy will sound large or modest depending on which is chosen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Multi-year totals do particular work. A commitment presented as a sum over five years is a larger number than the same commitment stated per year, and it is also harder to compare with anything, which is part of its appeal.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The baseline is chosen as well. An increase measured against a planned reduction is an increase; the same figure measured against last year's actual spending may be a cut, and both descriptions can be defended.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The speech also uses a particular tense. We are investing, we are backing, we are delivering, all present continuous, which describes a decision that has been taken as an action that is under way.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Independent analysis appears within hours, and the speech is written knowing that. The most contestable claims are often placed in the published documents rather than said aloud, because a sentence in an annex attracts less scrutiny than one in a broadcast.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric is about sequence and framing rather than about assertion, which is what makes it hard to rebut. Almost nothing in a budget speech is false, and the question worth asking of each sentence is what alternative description of the same figure was available and was not used.
