note: Pairs with How a Budget Is Assembled in this grade. One shows the process and the other the performance, and the performance is the only part most people see.

title: How a Risk Is Communicated
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A public health body has to tell people about a risk. The underlying number is the same whatever is said, and the way it is expressed changes what people decide to do, which makes the choice of expression a decision rather than a presentation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Percentages are poorly understood by many readers and frequencies are understood better. Ten in a thousand and one per cent describe the same quantity, and the first is consistently easier for people to reason with.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Keeping the denominator constant matters as much as the format. Comparing one in a hundred with one in a thousand requires an extra step that many readers do not take, while ten in a thousand against one in a thousand does not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Framing changes the decision even when the numbers are identical. A treatment described as having a ninety per cent survival rate is chosen more often than one described as having a ten per cent mortality rate, and this has been demonstrated repeatedly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That finding puts a communicator in an awkward position. There is no neutral framing available: survival and mortality are both accurate, one of them has to be chosen, and the choice will affect what people do.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The usual response is to give both, which helps and does not solve it. Order still matters, the first framing anchors the reader, and a document that presents both has made a smaller version of the same decision.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Visual formats carry their own effects. An array of a hundred figures with ten shaded conveys a proportion more reliably than a percentage, and a graph with a cut axis can make the same difference look like anything at all.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric here is unavoidable rather than optional. A communicator cannot decline to frame, and the honest position is to state which framing was chosen and why, rather than to present a choice as a fact.

title: The Recruitment Campaign
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Organisations that need people to join them, and that cannot compete on pay with the employers those people could otherwise choose, have to advertise something else. Armed forces, police services, teaching and nursing all run campaigns built on the same small number of appeals, in roughly the same order.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is belonging. The imagery is almost always of groups rather than individuals, and the implied offer is membership of something with a boundary around it, which is an offer competing employers find difficult to match.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is significance. The work is presented as mattering to other people in a way most work does not, and this appeal is powerful precisely because it is frequently true.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is transformation. A campaign shows a person at the end of training who is visibly not the person who began it, which is an offer about identity rather than about employment.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What is systematically absent is the ordinary content of the job. Very few campaigns show the paperwork, the shift patterns, the waiting, or the proportion of the work that is administrative, because those do not recruit anybody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That omission has a measurable consequence organisations track closely. Recruits who joined expecting the advertised version leave at higher rates when they meet the actual one, and the cost of early attrition is borne by the same organisation that ran the campaign.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some campaigns have responded by showing the difficulty deliberately. A campaign that emphasises how hard the work is can recruit fewer people and retain more of them, which is a better outcome and a harder one to defend to whoever counts applications.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric contains a tension the organisation cannot resolve by choosing better words. One metric rewards the appealing version and another punishes it, and the campaign is written for whichever metric the people commissioning it are judged on.

title: The Science Museum Label
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A label beside an object in a museum is usually under seventy-five words. It has to work for a reader who is standing, tired, possibly with a child, and who will give it about ten seconds before moving on.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Every constraint pushes in the same direction. There is no room for qualification, no room for competing accounts, and no room to explain why the object is in a museum rather than somewhere else.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What the label chooses to say the object is for is the heart of it. The same instrument can be introduced as a tool for measuring something, as evidence in a historical dispute, or as an example of a technique, and each produces a different visit.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A label also decides which person appears. Scientific instruments were generally built by named makers, used by named researchers and operated by assistants whose names are frequently recorded somewhere and almost never on the label.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The verbs carry a position. Was discovered, was developed and was first measured each distribute credit differently, and a label using the passive throughout has made a choice about agency that a visitor will not notice.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a genuine argument for the restraint. A museum that explains every dispute produces a wall of text nobody reads, and a visitor who leaves having understood one thing clearly has had a better visit than one who skimmed four arguments.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The cost falls on what cannot be shown. An object is a thing that survived, and a gallery of surviving objects is a gallery of what was built well, kept carefully and considered worth retaining, which is not the same as what was typical.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric of a label is mostly in its silences. The sentences present are generally accurate, and the argument is carried by what has been left out in order to fit seventy-five words.

questions.a: The same instrument can be introduced as a tool for measuring something, as evidence in a historical dispute, or as an example of a technique, and each produces a different visit.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the argument for restraint) and paragraph G (i.e. what a gallery of surviving objects represents).
Summarize how a museum label argues.
questions.a: Under seventy-five words and ten seconds of attention, a label has no room for qualification or competing accounts, so its choice of what the object is for shapes the visit, as do the people it names and the verbs that distribute credit. agency: who is represented as having acted, which the choice of verb distributes.

paras.text: The drawing is the legal and constructive document. It is dimensioned, it is to scale, and a contractor builds from it, which means that anything not drawn is not going to be built and any error in it becomes a wall in the wrong place.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.label: H

title: A War in Photographs and Statistics
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A conflict is described by photographs and by numbers, and the two accounts are so different in what they can carry that they are frequently read as contradicting each other when they do not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A photograph is a record of one place at one moment, and its strength is that it cannot be argued with about what was in front of the lens. It establishes that this happened, to this person, here.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It cannot establish how often. A single image of a destroyed street is compatible with one destroyed street or ten thousand, and a viewer has no way to tell which from the photograph itself.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Statistics answer exactly that question and lose everything else. A figure for displaced people describes a scale no photograph can convey, and it describes nobody in particular, which is a loss as well as a gain.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both are produced under conditions worth knowing. Photographs come from where photographers could reach, which is where access was granted or where danger was survivable, and the places nobody could reach are not photographed at all. An absence of images from a region is evidence about access rather than about what happened there.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Casualty figures come from whoever was counting, and counting during a conflict is done by parties with positions. Different methods produce different totals, and the difference between an estimate from records and an estimate from a survey is frequently large.

paras.label: G
paras.text: They also fail in opposite directions. A photograph can be unrepresentative while being entirely genuine, and a statistic can be accurate while describing a category that nobody would recognise as the thing they were asking about.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the honest reading uses each for what it establishes. The photograph is evidence that something occurred and poor evidence of how common it was, and the number is the reverse, and a reader with only one of them has half the account.

title: A Protein in Three Forms
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A protein can be presented as a sequence of letters, as a three-dimensional structure and as an animation of it working. The three are derived from each other and they support completely different kinds of reasoning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sequence is the most compact and the most certain. It is a string of letters representing amino acids in order, it can be stored and searched, and comparing two sequences reveals relationships between organisms that nothing else shows as cheaply.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is also nearly uninformative about function. The sequence determines the structure in principle, and reading function from it directly is close to impossible, which is why structure had to be determined experimentally for decades.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A structure answers what the sequence cannot. It shows the folded shape, the pocket where another molecule binds, and the surfaces that face outward, and almost everything a drug designer needs is a property of the shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A structure is also a model rather than a photograph. It is fitted to experimental data, parts of it are less certain than others, and a published structure carries measures of that uncertainty which the picture of it does not. A loop region drawn as confidently as the rest may be the part nobody could resolve.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An animation adds the dimension both of the others lack. A protein is not rigid; it moves, and the motion is frequently the mechanism, so a static structure can be a correct picture of a thing whose behaviour it cannot show.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The animation is also the furthest from the evidence. Most such films are built from a small number of structures plus simulation plus choices about pacing and colour, and a viewer cannot tell which parts were measured and which were plausible.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So confidence runs opposite to vividness. The sequence is most certain and least illuminating, the animation is most illuminating and least constrained, and the structure sits between them, which is why all three are published together.

title: An Economy in Three Accounts
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An economy is described by aggregate figures, by charts and by individual accounts of how people are living. The three are usually presented as competing, and they are answering questions that do not overlap.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An aggregate figure such as total output is the only thing that permits comparison. It allows one year to be set against another and one country against another, and nothing else available does that at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It conceals distribution completely, and this is not a subtle defect. A total that rises while most people's incomes fall is arithmetically ordinary, and the figure reports the rise accurately and says nothing about the fall.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A chart adds the shape of a change over time, which a single number cannot carry. It shows whether something is accelerating, whether it has recovered and whether a recent movement is unusual against its own history.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A chart's design decisions are substantial. The period chosen determines what counts as normal, the axis determines how large a change looks, and whether a figure is shown per person or in total can reverse the direction of the line.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An individual account carries what neither can. It describes what a change consists of for a household, in terms of what is bought, what is postponed and what is given up, and that is the only form in which a number becomes legible.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It establishes nothing about how common it is. A single household's experience is compatible with it being universal or rare, which is the limitation a reporter addresses by choosing a household described as typical, on a judgement the reader cannot check.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the useful arrangement is all three in a known order. The aggregate says how much, the chart says in what pattern, the account says what it consists of, and each of them is misleading in a predictable way when it appears alone.

title: A Species as Specimen, Photograph and Recording
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A newly described animal is documented in three ways at once, and each of the three answers a question the others cannot answer at all, which is why a modern description includes all of them wherever the describing team is able to.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The specimen is the anchor. It is a physical individual, preserved and deposited, and it remains available for measurement by people who were not born when it was collected and who have instruments nobody then imagined.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That permanence is what distinguishes it absolutely. A specimen collected in 1890 can now be sampled for genetic material and examined by scanning, so a decision made then is still producing evidence that nobody could have intended.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its limitation is equally absolute. A specimen is dead, it has usually been altered by preservation, and the colours of many organisms begin changing within hours of death, so a drawer records shape far better than appearance.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A photograph answers appearance and behaviour. It shows posture, living colour, what the animal was doing and the habitat around it, and all of that is lost from a specimen before the specimen reaches a collection.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It records only what was pointed at. A photograph is taken by someone who decided what mattered, from where they could stand, and the feature a later researcher wants is frequently just outside the frame. Nothing in the image indicates that it was ever there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A recording answers what neither can, and for many groups it is decisive. Species of bird, frog and insect that are visually almost identical are separated reliably by sound, and the sound is a behaviour rather than a structure.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the three divide along a clear line. The specimen holds structure permanently, the photograph holds appearance at a moment, the recording holds behaviour, and a description with only the first is unable to distinguish species that a listener can tell apart in a field.

title: Survivorship Bias
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study of successful companies identifies the habits they share and recommends those habits to everybody else. The reasoning seems unimpeachable at first reading: the data are real, the habits were measured carefully, and the companies in question did in fact succeed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The error is in which companies were available to measure. The study examined the ones that still existed, and a company that adopted the same habits and failed was not in the sample because it was not there to be studied.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That omission can produce any conclusion at all. If a habit is common among both survivors and failures, examining only survivors makes it look like a cause of success, when it may be a cause of nothing or a cause of failure.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The classic case concerns aircraft returning from missions in the Second World War, inspected to decide where to add armour. The returning planes showed damage concentrated in certain areas, and the obvious response was to armour those areas.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Abraham Wald's observation was that the sample consisted of aircraft that came back. Damage in those areas was survivable by definition, and the places with no damage on returning aircraft were the places where a hit meant the plane did not return.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The correction is counterintuitive in a specific way. The right response was to armour exactly where the data showed no damage, which inverts the apparent reading of a perfectly accurate dataset.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Identifying it in a new case requires asking a particular question before looking at any figures: what would have had to happen for a case to be absent from this data, and is that thing related to what is being measured?

paras.label: H
paras.text: Where the answer is yes, the dataset cannot support the conclusion however large it is. Adding more survivors adds more of the same selection, and a confident finding from a complete census of survivors is still a finding about survival.

Wald showed that armour belonged where returning aircraft showed no damage, and detection requires asking what would make a case absent and whether that is related to what is being measured.

sample: the cases actually examined, which may have been selected by the very thing being studied.
selection: the process determining which cases are available, which can produce a bias no amount of data removes.

questions.a: Adding more survivors adds more of the same selection, so a confident finding from a complete census of survivors is still a finding about survival.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A claim is put forward and someone objects that if it were true, something bad would follow from it. The objection is often entirely sincere, it is frequently persuasive to an audience, and it is not an argument about whether the claim is true.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The structure is easy to state and harder to notice in use. We cannot accept this, because accepting it would mean accepting that, and the second clause describes a consequence rather than offering evidence.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It appears in both directions. If this result holds, decades of work were wasted, and if this result holds, our approach is vindicated, are the same move, and the second is less often challenged because the people making it are pleased.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is a legitimate neighbour that must not be confused with it. If a claim implies something already known to be false, that is a genuine argument against the claim, because a true statement cannot entail a false one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distinction is between implying something false and implying something unwelcome. The first is a logical relation and the second is an assessment of consequences, and an argument slides between them easily because both begin the same way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a legitimate use in deciding what to do. If a claim might be true and acting on it would be catastrophic, the consequence is a sound reason to act cautiously, and it remains no reason at all to believe the claim is false.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That separation is the whole of it. What is true and what it would be convenient to be true are different questions, and the appeal collapses them so smoothly that a listener can agree without noticing a question has been swapped.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The test is therefore mechanical. Remove the clause describing what would follow, and ask whether anything remains that bears on whether the claim is correct, and frequently nothing does.

title: The Pattern Drawn Afterwards
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study measures many things at once and reports the one that came out striking. Nothing has been fabricated, every measurement was really taken, and the conclusion is still unreliable in a way that cannot be detected by reading the paper alone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The arithmetic is the reason. If twenty independent comparisons are made and the usual threshold is applied, roughly one is expected to pass it by chance even where nothing whatever is going on.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A paper reporting that one comparison has reported a true measurement. What it has not reported is how many others were made, and without that number a reader cannot tell a finding from a lottery result.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The name usually given to this comes from a story about a marksman who fires at a barn and then paints a target around the tightest cluster of holes. The shooting is genuine and the accuracy is created afterwards.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It arises most naturally in subgroup analysis. A treatment showing no overall effect may show one in men over sixty, and if twelve subgroups were examined the appearance of one such result is what chance alone predicts. The published paper frequently names only that subgroup.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The correction is not to forbid such analysis, which would discard real discoveries. It is to state in advance which comparison is the main one, and to treat everything else as a question for a later study rather than as a finding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is what registration provides, and it is why the gap between a registered protocol and a published paper is so informative. A main outcome that changed between the two is a specific and checkable event.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The underlying lesson is uncomfortable. A striking result from a study that looked at many things is weaker evidence than an unremarkable result from a study that looked at one, and nothing visible in the two papers shows that.

title: The Slippery Slope
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.

 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An argument against a proposal says that allowing it will lead to something nobody wants. The chain may be three steps or ten, and the form is the same: not this is bad, but this leads to that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form is not automatically fallacious, which is why it is difficult. Some chains are real, institutions do set precedents, and an argument that a measure will be extended is sometimes a correct prediction with evidence behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What distinguishes a sound version is that each step is defended. A claim that A leads to B requires a reason why, and a claim that B leads to C requires another, and an argument that asserts the chain without supporting the links has asserted a story.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Probability compounds in a way intuition handles badly. If each of five steps is eighty per cent likely, the whole chain is about a third likely, and an argument that feels overwhelming step by step may be unlikely taken whole.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fallacious version also tends to describe the final step vividly and the intermediate ones briefly. Attention is drawn to the destination, which is doing emotional work, and away from the links, which is where the argument would have to be checked.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A useful counter-question is whether the intermediate steps have independent defences. If step three would be opposed on its own terms by the same people and institutions, then arriving at it is not automatic and the chain has a stopping point.

paras.label: G
paras.text: History supplies cases in both directions, which is why neither side can settle this generally. Some measures were extended exactly as predicted, and others were adopted and not extended for decades, and pointing at either set proves nothing about a new case.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the assessment has to be specific. Name the steps, ask what evidence supports each transition, and ask what would prevent it, and an argument that cannot answer those about step two has not earned step seven.

title: Absence of Evidence
standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A search finds nothing, and two opposite conclusions are drawn from the same result. One side says this shows the thing does not exist, the other says this shows nothing at all, and both are sometimes right.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The phrase absence of evidence is not evidence of absence is widely quoted and is only half true. Whether an absence is informative depends entirely on how hard anyone looked and on what they would have found.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A search that would certainly have detected the thing, and did not, is strong evidence that the thing is not there. That is an ordinary and sound inference, and it is what a negative medical test is for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A search that might have missed it says far less, and how much less is calculable rather than a matter of opinion. The quantity is the probability of finding the thing if it were present, which is what a study's power measures.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the question to ask of any negative result is never whether something was found. It is what the search would have detected, and a report that does not state that has not reported enough to be interpreted either way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The error runs in both directions and the second is less often noticed. Treating a weak search as decisive overstates it; treating a powerful search as uninformative because absence is not evidence is a misuse of a slogan to dismiss a real finding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: An example makes the asymmetry concrete. If a careful survey of a small island reports no large mammals, that is strong evidence, and if the same method is applied once to a continent it establishes very little.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The slogan survives because it is a useful correction to one specific error. Used as a general principle it licenses ignoring any negative result at all, which is the opposite of what the people who coined it were arguing for.

title: The Preamble to the Constitution
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Constitution of the United States opens with a single sentence of fifty-two words, and nearly every phrase in it was contested by the people who agreed to it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first three words are the most argued over. We the People locates the authority of the document in a population rather than in the states that sent delegates, and an earlier draft had begun by naming the states individually.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That change was partly practical. The document would take effect when nine states ratified, so naming thirteen would have been inaccurate the moment it was signed, and the general formulation avoided the problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It was not only practical, and both sides understood that. If the authority comes from a people, then the union is not an agreement among states that states might revisit, and the question of who the parties were is not settled by the text.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The purposes that follow are a list of six, and they are not in a random order. A more perfect union comes first, justice and domestic tranquillity next, the common defence after that, and the general welfare and liberty last.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The phrase to form a more perfect union is doing quiet work. It concedes that a union already existed under the Articles of Confederation and claims that this document improves rather than replaces it, which was the politically necessary claim.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The preamble creates no powers and grants no rights, and courts have long held that nothing can be founded on it alone. It is a statement of purpose, and its legal function is to inform the reading of the clauses that follow.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Declaration, the difference in task is visible immediately. The Declaration argues that a government may be dissolved, and the Preamble states what a government is being constituted to do, and the same people wrote both within eleven years.

title: Federalist Number Ten
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Federalist papers were written to persuade New York to ratify the Constitution. They are advocacy, published under a pseudonym, and the tenth of them is the most studied because it answers the strongest objection the other side had.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That objection came from accepted theory. Republics were understood to work only in small territories, because a large and diverse population would contain too many competing interests for any common good to emerge.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Madison accepts the premise about interests and reverses the conclusion. He argues that faction is not a defect to be eliminated but a permanent consequence of liberty, since people free to think differently will form groups around different interests.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument that follows turns on what can be done about it. Removing the causes of faction would require destroying liberty or making everyone think alike, and both remedies are described as worse than the disease.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the question becomes how to control the effects. A minority faction can be outvoted, which leaves the hard case: a faction that constitutes a majority, which cannot be outvoted and which ordinary republican machinery does not restrain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The solution is where the essay inverts the received view entirely. In a large republic there are more interests, so a majority is harder to assemble, and any majority that forms must be built from groups that agree about less.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The size that was supposed to be fatal therefore becomes the protection. The essay is not arguing that a large republic is tolerable despite being large; it is arguing that it is safer than a small one, for the reason small ones were praised.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Preamble, the two do different halves of one job. The Preamble states what the union is for, and this essay argues why an institution of that size could achieve it, which is the claim the Preamble assumes and does not defend.

title: The Bill of Rights
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution were ratified in 1791, four years after the document they amend was signed. Their existence is the result of an argument that the original text had lost, and the terms of that argument are still visible in how they are written.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Several states had ratified the Constitution only on the understanding that amendments protecting individual rights would follow. Without that understanding the document would probably not have been adopted, and the amendments are therefore part of the price of ratification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument against them was not that rights do not matter. Hamilton argued in Federalist 84 that a list would be dangerous, because enumerating some rights implies that the ones not listed were not protected.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That objection was taken seriously enough to be answered inside the text. The Ninth Amendment states that listing certain rights shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people, which is a clause written to answer an argument.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The drafting is also notable for what it restrains. Most of the amendments limit what government may do rather than describing what a person may do, so the First begins with a prohibition on Congress rather than a grant to a speaker.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That form matters for how they were originally understood. A restriction on Congress is a restriction on the federal government, and applying these limits to states happened much later, through a long sequence of decisions under the Fourteenth Amendment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The Tenth closes the set by stating a principle about everything unstated. Powers not delegated to the federal government, and not prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states or to the people.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside Federalist Ten, the two sit uneasily together, which is the interesting part. One argues that structure and scale are what protect liberty, and the other was demanded by people who did not find that argument sufficient.

title: Lincoln's Second Inaugural
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Lincoln's second inaugural address, delivered in March 1865, is about seven hundred words long. The war was nearly over, his side was going to win, and the speech does almost nothing that the occasion would predict.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It does not claim victory, name a general or describe a battle. It spends its first third on the situation four years earlier, in the measured tone of a man recounting something both audiences already knew.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then names the cause of the war directly, which the first inaugural had not. Slavery is identified as the interest over which the parties divided, and the sentence is constructed so that no reader can take it as referring to anything else.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The section that follows is the strangest and the most carefully built. It observes that both sides read the same Bible, pray to the same God, and each invokes that God's aid against the other.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The symmetry is doing deliberate work. By placing the two sides in the same sentence, with the same practices, the speech removes the usual structure of a victory address, in which one side is the subject and the other is the problem.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The passage then declines to resolve the symmetry in his own favour. Lincoln says that the prayers of neither have been answered fully, and that the Almighty has his own purposes, which is a refusal to claim divine endorsement at a moment when it was available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The closing is the most quoted and is frequently detached from what precedes it. With malice toward none, with charity for all follows an argument that has already refused to describe the enemy as different in kind.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Gettysburg Address, the pair shows the same method at two scales. One dates a nation to make a claim about its principle, and the other describes a war without an enemy to make a claim about what follows it.

title: What the Emancipation Proclamation Did
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on the first of January, 1863, in the middle of a war whose outcome was not yet decided. It is among the most famous documents in American history and among the most frequently misdescribed, because what it actually did and what it is remembered for are not the same thing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It did not abolish slavery. It declared enslaved people free in the areas then in rebellion, and it explicitly exempted the border states that had remained in the Union and the parts of the Confederacy already under federal control.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That exemption produced the obvious objection at the time and since. The proclamation freed people in the places where the federal government had no power to free anyone and left slavery untouched where it did.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The legal reasoning behind the exemption is the explanation. The document was issued as a war measure under the president's authority as commander in chief, which could reach enemy property in a rebellion and could not reach a loyal state.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So its immediate effect was conditional on military advance. As federal armies took territory, the proclamation applied there, which made every advance an act of emancipation and gave the army a function it had not previously had.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It also changed who could fight. The proclamation authorised the enlistment of Black soldiers in the United States forces, and roughly two hundred thousand served, which altered the manpower position and the meaning of the war simultaneously.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The international effect is frequently overlooked and was substantial. After January 1863 the war was explicitly about slavery, which made recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible for European governments whose populations opposed it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, which is the document that did the thing the proclamation is remembered for. Read together they show a familiar pattern: the famous text changed the terms, and a less famous one changed the law.

title: The Eclipse That Tested a Theory
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: General relativity predicted in 1915 that gravity bends light, and predicted a specific amount: twice the deflection that Newtonian reasoning gives for a star's light passing the edge of the sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The prediction was testable only under one circumstance. The sun's own light drowns the stars beside it, so the only way to photograph them is during a total eclipse, and the only way to measure a shift is to compare that photograph with one of the same stars months later.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two expeditions went out in May 1919, one to Príncipe off West Africa and one to Sobral in Brazil, organised in Britain by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson. The war had ended six months earlier.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The measurement is extremely difficult and the numbers involved are tiny. The expected shift is a fraction of a second of arc, which required photographic plates compared with instruments operating close to their limits.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The conditions were poor. Príncipe was clouded for most of totality, and of the plates taken there only two were usable; Sobral had better weather and one of its two instruments produced images affected by heating of the mirror.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The results were announced in November 1919 and reported worldwide as a confirmation. The Príncipe plates and the better Sobral instrument agreed with Einstein's figure, and the problematic Sobral instrument gave a value closer to the Newtonian one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The handling of that third dataset has been argued about ever since. It was given less weight on the stated ground that the instrument was known to have a defect, which is a legitimate reason and is also what one would say if one wanted a particular answer.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Later measurements settled the question independently and repeatedly, which is why the episode is now interesting for a different reason. It is a case where the conclusion was right, the data were marginal, and a judgement was made that only subsequent work could justify.

title: The Manuscripts of Timbuktu
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, was a centre of scholarship for several centuries, with universities and a trade in books. It held libraries of manuscripts written in Arabic and in African languages using Arabic script, covering astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law, poetry and the practical business of commerce.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The existence of those manuscripts contradicts a claim that was once widely made. Written scholarship in West Africa before European contact was frequently denied, and the denial survived partly because the evidence was held in private family collections rather than in public institutions.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That privacy was a preservation strategy rather than secrecy for its own sake. Collections passed down within families were kept out of sight during periods when they might have been seized or destroyed, and the same practice preserved them and kept them unavailable to anyone attempting to catalogue what existed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Estimates of the number run to hundreds of thousands across the region, and the range is wide because many have never been seen by anyone outside the family holding them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Their physical condition is the permanent problem. The climate is hostile to paper, insects are a continuous threat, and a manuscript that has survived four hundred years in a chest may not survive being moved, opened or photographed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2012, when armed groups took control of the city, a large-scale evacuation was organised. Manuscripts were packed into footlockers and moved out by road and by river over several months, in an operation that depended on secrecy.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The evacuation saved an enormous number and created a second problem immediately. Material that had been stable in a dry northern climate was moved to a humid southern one, where the threat is mould rather than seizure.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode shows a tension that applies to any endangered archive. Material survives by being left alone and becomes useful by being catalogued and read, and every act that makes a collection accessible also makes it more vulnerable.

title: The Island That Rose From the Sea
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In November 1963 a volcanic eruption began on the sea floor south of Iceland, was first noticed by the crew of a fishing boat, and continued for more than three years. What emerged from it was an entirely new island, named Surtsey, covering about two and a half square kilometres at its largest.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A new island is an unusual scientific opportunity because it supplies something that is otherwise impossible to obtain: a surface of known age with nothing living on it, in a region where the surrounding biology is thoroughly documented.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Iceland protected it almost immediately. Landing is restricted to a small number of researchers, nothing may be brought ashore that could introduce an organism, and the island has been surveyed on a schedule ever since.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The arrivals were recorded in order, which is the entire value of the exercise. Bacteria and fungi were present early, the first vascular plant was found in 1965, mosses followed, and lichens appeared several years after that.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Birds changed the rate decisively. Gulls began nesting in 1986, and the area around their colony developed vegetation far faster than the rest of the island, because the birds brought both seeds and the nutrients plants needed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a result nobody could have obtained from a mature ecosystem. The causal relationship between seabird colonies and plant establishment is visible at Surtsey because the before state was observed rather than inferred.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The island is also eroding, and faster than it formed. Much of the original area has been lost to the sea, and the long-term projection is that what remains will be a small core of harder material.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The protection is therefore the experiment. A single unauthorised landing with a seed on a boot would not destroy the island and would destroy the record, which is why the restriction is absolute and why it has held for sixty years.

questions.q:
vascular plant: a plant with tissue for conducting water, distinguishing it from mosses and lichens.
colonisation: the arrival and establishment of organisms on ground that held none.
Describe the connection between the landing restriction and the value of the data.
questions.a: A single unauthorised landing with a seed on a boot would not destroy the island and would destroy the record, which is why the restriction is absolute.

note: An experiment whose method is a prohibition. Ask what the island would be worth scientifically if visitors had been allowed in 1964.

title: The Village That Shut Its Gates
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1665 plague reached the village of Eyam in Derbyshire, probably carried in a consignment of cloth sent from London. Over the following fourteen months a substantial proportion of the inhabitants died, in a community small enough that the dead were known individually to everyone left.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What is remembered about Eyam is the decision that followed. The villagers agreed to isolate themselves, not to leave, and to accept supplies left at boundary stones, in order to prevent the disease spreading to surrounding settlements.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The account rests on a mixture of sources of very different quality. Parish burial registers are contemporary and reliable; the narrative of a collective decision rests substantially on accounts written considerably later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That distinction matters because the two support different claims. The registers establish who died and when, with dates, and the later accounts establish what people in the following century believed about why.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Historians have used the registers for something the villagers could not have intended and would not have recognised as a use. The burial dates, combined with surviving records of which households stood where and who lived in them, allow transmission within the village to be reconstructed with unusual precision.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The results have revised the traditional picture in a specific way. Mortality varied enormously between households, and the pattern is more consistent with transmission within families and dwellings than with a single uniform exposure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The quarantine's effectiveness is harder to assess and is genuinely disputed among historians. Surrounding villages were not devastated, which is consistent with the isolation having worked and equally consistent with several other explanations that nobody is now in a position to exclude.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So Eyam supports two claims of different strength, and conflating them is the usual error. That a community isolated itself and that many died is well evidenced; that the isolation saved the surrounding region is a reasonable inference and not a demonstrated fact.

title: The Signal That Came From a Microwave
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Radio telescopes at Parkes in Australia had for some years been recording occasional bursts of radio energy lasting only milliseconds. Some of them were genuinely astronomical and are now an established field of study, and some belonged to a second category that behaved strangely from the beginning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The strange ones were given their own name, perytons. They appeared at roughly the right frequencies, they were short, and they looked enough like the real signals that distinguishing them was not immediately possible.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Several features did not fit. Perytons were detected across the whole sky rather than from a direction, which is not how an astronomical source behaves, and they clustered around the middle of the day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also came in groups. A single astronomical event does not repeat on a schedule, and perytons tended to arrive in clusters separated by minutes, which pointed clearly at a terrestrial source without doing anything at all to identify which one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The investigation took years and was not glamorous at any point. A radio-frequency interference monitor was installed at the site, and the team then waited for a peryton to occur while that second instrument was running and recording everything else happening nearby.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2015 they found it. The signals were produced by the kitchen microwave ovens in the observatory building, and specifically by a door being opened before the timer finished, which stops the magnetron mid-cycle and releases a brief burst.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The clustering around midday was lunch. The whole-sky detection was because the source was inside the building rather than in a direction, and the resemblance to real bursts was a coincidence of frequency and duration.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is not a failure, and it is told as one too often. The team suspected a local source for years, investigated systematically and eventually identified it, which is what an instrument's noise characterisation is supposed to do.

questions.a: The signals were detected across the whole sky rather than from a direction because the source was inside the building rather than at a point in space.

note: Closes the grade on the same discipline it opened with at Penzias and Wilson in grade 9: eliminating what the instrument itself is doing before claiming anything about the sky.
